prose.def: An enclitic particle that adds emphasis or force to the word it attaches to, meaning something like "indeed" or "by far."
prose.article: "Per" is a small enclitic particle that never stands alone — it always attaches to another word to strengthen or sharpen it, adding a sense of "indeed" or "by far." You meet it embedded in familiar compounds like "hosper" and "kathaper" ("just as"), "kaiper" ("although"), and "eiper" ("if indeed"). Abbott-Smith notes it is akin to "peri" and in the New Testament is always affixed to a preceding word rather than used independently.
prose.caution: There are no measured senses because the particle never appears on its own in the Byzantine New Testament — it survives only inside compound words.

prose.article: περισσός points to something that exceeds the normal amount or standard—whether "more" in quantity or "greater" in rank. prose.article: πιπράσκω means to sell, to dispose of goods or people as merchandise. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 9 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sold" in all 8 cases where it gets its own English word — a remarkably consistent pattern. It can carry the harder edge of selling a person into slavery (Matthew 18:25) and even speak figuratively, as in Romans 7:14. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this commercial sense vividly: one document from 159 B.C. uses the very same perfect form found in Matthew 13:46 to record "I have sold" a piece of linen for a sum of drachmas.

prose.article: πίπτω means to fall in nearly every sense: things dropping, people collapsing, or someone falling prostrate before another in worship or supplication. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "fell" in 80 of its 90 New Testament occurrences (98%), and the lexicons agree this covers both literal descent and figurative falling, such as falling under judgment. A nice detail from the everyday papyri: the form πέπτωκεν was common business shorthand meaning "paid," as in money that has "fallen" onto a bank's table.

prose.def: Pisidia, a mountainous region in southern Asia Minor forming the south-western part of the Roman province of Galatia; Antioch lay near, not strictly within, this region.
prose.article: Pisidia is a place name for a mountainous region in southern Asia Minor, mentioned twice in the New Testament (Acts 13:14 and 14:24). The two occurrences split evenly between referring to the region itself ("Pisidia") and describing "Pisidian Antioch" as inland. Notably, Moulton-Milligan and the scholar Ramsay point out that Pisidian Antioch was actually near Pisidia rather than strictly within it, which is why the city carried the regional label.

prose.def: To believe or trust a person or claim, or (passive) to be entrusted with something; especially, to place active, ongoing faith in God or Christ.
prose.article: πιστεύω overwhelmingly means "believe"—the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way 220 times (98%), and the Berean Standard Bible independently agrees at the same rate. Its range stretches from simply accepting that something is true to actively placing one's trust in a person, which is why it can also shade into "entrust" (as the passive "be entrusted with"). In the Septuagint it almost always stands in for the Hebrew אָמַן (36 of 48 times), the word behind ideas of firmness and faithfulness; the everyday papyri show the same construction "believe someone" used in ordinary documents.
